transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-05
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Sunrise CTO), Maya Patel (Platform Eng), Jordan Reyes (DevOps)

Summary (auto): Quickstart SDK walkthrough focusing on auth and environment setup; demo of console tokens; discuss pilot benchmarks and security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. Priya our SE is with me. Quick roll call?
[00:00:10] Liam: Liam here, hi.
[00:00:12] Maya: Maya, platform team.
[00:00:14] Jordan: Jordan, DevOps.
[00:00:16] Priya: Priya Kapoor, SE at Redwood. Nice to meet you all.
[00:00:20] Alex: Cool. The plan is a short overview, then a live SDK quickstart — python and typescript — then auth patterns and CI env set up. We'll keep it practical.
[00:00:35] Liam: Sounds good, our immediate goal is to get a PoC running in our sandbox within one week and then a small benchmark.
[00:00:40] Alex: Perfect. Priya, do you want to share your screen?
[00:00:45] Priya: Yep, sharing now. You'll see the Redwood Console, project landing page.
[00:00:52] [00:00:52] (screen share)
[00:00:55] Priya: On the left is Projects, Tokens, Models. For quickstarts we usually create a sandbox project and generate a token with least privilege. We'll show the python example from the quickstart repo.
[00:01:10] Maya: Quick question, token lifecycle — can tokens be scoped to routes or models?
[00:01:15] Priya: Currently token scopes include project-level and role based API keys; you can limit to only generate embeddings or generation. We also support short-lived keys and rotating via the Console or API. For stricter setups we recommend pairing with SSO provisioning and Redwood Private where tokens are ephemeral and bound to your identity provider.
[00:01:35] Jordan: And KMS? We need keys encrypted in transit and at rest, prefer customer-managed keys.
[00:01:41] Priya: Yes, for Private we integrate with customer KMS or HSM, and for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys or bring-your-own key via KMS integration. We'll drop the security doc after the call.
[00:01:55] Alex: Ok jumping into the repo: pip install redwood-sdk (note: package name in rapid demo might be illustrative).
[00:02:05] Priya: The python snippet — set environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY, then from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(); resp = client.generate("Write a product blurb..."). The TS example uses env var process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY and the @redwood/sdk client.
[00:02:25] Liam: Do you have sample CI patterns? We want to avoid committing keys to repos and ensure ephemeral tokens for CI jobs.
[00:02:31] Priya: Yes — we recommend using secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager/GCP Secret Manager) or GitHub Actions secrets, and fetch ephemeral tokens via service account with limited scope. Many customers set up a service account that mints a short-lived project token via Redwood API. We'll share a sample GitHub Actions snippet.
[00:02:50] Jordan: Nice. For our on-prem runners we have no internet egress for some jobs, how do you suggest testing?
[00:02:57] Priya: For strict egress we do private deployment or VPC connector. But for quick PoC you can run a proxy in a DMZ or use a developer machine with egress. Also we support an on-prem package if you go that route.
[00:03:15] Maya: How about model pinning? We want predictable behavior between dev and prod.
[00:03:20] Priya: Pin model versions in the client config or in your route config in Console. That way dev, staging and prod reference the same model sha/tag and you control rollouts.
[00:03:30] Alex: Let's run a quick python demo — I'll paste command lines into chat.
[00:03:35] [00:03:35] Alex: (typing) virtualenv venv && source venv/bin/activate
[00:03:45] Alex: pip install redwood-sdk==0.8.1 (note: example pinned).
[00:03:52] Priya: Then export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-sandbox-xxxx (we'll provide the real key). Example code: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); print(client.generate('Summarize last meeting notes'))
[00:04:12] [00:04:12] Maya: I'm seeing a note in the docs about batching and token cost, can you explain Optimize recommendations briefly?
[00:04:18] Priya: Sure — Redwood Optimize suggests batching, shorter seq lengths, and quantized model variants for cost sensitive workloads. For chat UI we recommend prefix caching and KV cache reuse to reduce repeated context cost. The Console has a Optimize tab with recommendations per route.
[00:04:35] Liam: Would that affect latency? We need sub-300ms tail for some flows.
[00:04:38] Priya: There's always a tradeoff. Batching improves throughput but can increase single-request latency unless you use dynamic batching thresholds with a latency SLO. For strict latency we recommend Dedicated capacity in the right GPU profile and smaller model variants.
[00:04:55] Jordan: Any rough numbers for 8k seq?
[00:04:58] Priya: Depends on model & GPU. We'll run a small benchmark — for instance on an A100 quantized variant you might see X tokens/sec — we'll provide a spreadsheet with baseline numbers.
[00:05:15] Alex: Back to auth patterns — we had a question about SAML/SSO provisioning for token issuance.
[00:05:21] Priya: Redwood supports SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and role-based access control. For programmatic tokens we recommend short lived tokens minted by a service account; that bridges SSO-managed identities with API usage. Some customers use GitHub OIDC to mint ephemeral tokens in CI.
[00:05:40] Liam: Great. For our security team, can you share audit log retention and per-token usage logs?
[00:05:45] Priya: Yes — structured audit logs available in Console and exportable to your SIEM; retention is configurable for Dedicated and Private, and hosted has default retention we can discuss. We'll include the logs doc.
[00:05:58] Maya: Quick thing — you mentioned KV cash earlier in a doc, I think you mean KV cache?
[00:06:03] Priya: Yes sorry, KV cache, my bad — transcription in some docs shows cash, ha.
[00:06:10] [00:06:10] (light laugh)
[00:06:15] Alex: Ok let's also walk through the TS sample. Priya, you can show the node example.
[00:06:20] Priya: Sure — npx create-sample; npm install @redwood/sdk; then in .env: REDWOOD_API_KEY=... and REDWOOD_PROJECT=proj-sandbox. The client usage is similar. When running inside docker we mount env var through a runtime secret.
[00:06:40] Jordan: For our CI we prefer not to have long lived tokens in environment — is there a recommended rotate cadence?
[00:06:46] Priya: Rotate nightly for CI runners that run jobs, or use ephemeral tokens per job, generated by a small service that uses a service account with limited scope. We'll share an example service.
[00:06:58] Liam: Any gotchas for switching from a POC hosted plan to Dedicated later?
[00:07:05] Priya: Main considerations: data isolation and throughput. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and private pools; you'll want to pin model variants and adjust autoscaling policies. We can migrate routes and keep same API surface, minimal code change — mostly config.
[00:07:22] Alex: Alright, quick recap of what we'll send: sandbox API key + repo link, security docs, brief benchmark spreadsheet template.
[00:07:30] Liam: Good. Also can we get a note on pricing tiers for the dedicated baseline — rough numbers to show procurement?
[00:07:36] Alex: Yes I'll include ballpark reserved capacity pricing; formal quote via sales after pilot metrics.
[00:07:42] Maya: One last question — do you support function/tool calling or structured output? We want to call internal tools from responses.
[00:07:48] Priya: Yes we support function/tool calling patterns and structured JSON outputs. We have examples in the SDK quickstart.
[00:07:55] Jordan: Great.
[00:08:00] Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items. Any final questions?
[00:08:05] Liam: Not from me.
[00:08:07] Maya: All good.
[00:08:09] Jordan: Nope.
[00:08:11] Alex: Ok meeting wrap.
